title: CHAPTER THIRTEEN. On the mode and necessary consequence and end of the resurrection — namely the last judgment
english: CHAPTER THIRTEEN. On the mode and necessary consequence and end of the resurrection — namely the last judgment.
So far have been the causes of the resurrection; now follow its mode and necessary consequence and end.

II. The mode of the resurrection is not perfectly known — he who willed that not even of all natural things the modes and reasons be open to us. The mode can be reduced to the form explained in Cap. 12 aph. 6–7: gathering of dust, formation of the body, animation — but it is a mystery (1 Cor. 15:51; 1 Thess. 4:15).

title: III–IV. Necessary consequence is the last judgment; definition; Gentile inklings
english: III. The necessary consequence and end is the last judgment, and the condition of those judged.

IV. The last judgment is that most august act by which Christ, returning from heaven with highest glory and majesty at the end of this world, judges the whole orb of the earth. In the foundations of the Christian faith (Heb. 6:2) these two are joined. A general notion is implanted in all by nature, and a confused sense among the Gentiles — whether because they gathered that divine justice requires such a judgment, or from conscience, or because something of the Church's teaching reached their ears. That the dogma was revealed to the patriarchs the prophecy of Enoch shows (Jude 14–15).

title: V. Certainty of the day hidden; VI. Efficient cause — Trinity; Son visibly
english: V. Its existence as certainly future is on the last day of this world, hidden in the treasures of divine wisdom. Scriptures: Acts 17:31; Rom. 2:5; 2 Thess. 1; Matt. 24:36; 25:31. Detestable are the Borborians, Floriani, Manichees and Proclinianites who denied it. In vain we try to compute the years; Christ forbade it (Acts 1:7).

VI. The principal efficient cause is the Holy Trinity as to authority and power; the visible form and exercise is the Son of God in assumed human nature. To him is given all judgment (John 5:22, 27), all power (Matt. 28:18); he is appointed (Acts 17:31) — not as a delegated judge but as prince by appropriation. The saints enter partnership not as to authority in themselves, but inasmuch as in Christ the head they pronounce, approve, and testify by their life.

title: VII–IX. Matter: persons (angels and all humans) and all acts
english: VII. The matter or object of the last judgment is partly persons, partly their acts.

VIII. The persons are the evil angels and all humans both good and evil. The evil angels, already subject to punishments, will receive the complement on the last day. All humans living and dead will be judged — the good by a judgment of discernment and absolution, the evil of condemnation.

IX. The acts are all thoughts, inclinations, gestures, words, and deeds of all humans, with their principles, circumstances, and accidents. Their revelation is signified by the opening of the books (Rev. 20:12).

title: X–XI. Form of judgment in four parts; end — God's glory — Cap. 13 close
english: X. The form of this judgment is contained in (1) knowledge of the cause; (2) separation of those to be judged; (3) decision of the known cause and promulgation of the sentence; (4) execution of the sentence passed. In knowledge the judge needs no examination of witnesses. Separation of sheep from goats is Matt. 25:32–33. The sentence is most joyful for the pious, most sad for the impious. Execution is in public and solemn pronouncement, so that the just begin to enjoy beatitude consummately in heaven, and the impious to be punished without end in hell.

XI. The ultimate end of this judgment is that God be glorified in his saints and become wonderful in all who believed; subordinate ends are the salvation of the pious, the casting off of the impious, and the liberation of Christ's Church (2 Thess. 1:6–7).
